newsitem.title: USA: Dole envoy meets with Perot.
newsitem.headline: Dole envoy meets with Perot.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Republican challenger Bob Dole, lagging far behind President Bill Clinton in polls and running out of time, sent his campaign manager to meet Texas billionaire Ross Perot on Wednesday, a senior Reform Party official said.

Scott Reed and Perot talked "very briefly," the official said. He would not confirm television news reports that Reed had asked Perot to pull out of the contest for the White House and throw his support behind the Republican ticket.
"There is no way Ross is going to pull out of the race," the official said.
The Dole campaign refused to confirm the meeting had taken place. "I've got a hearing problem," Dole said in response to repeated questions from reporters in Panama City, Florida, Wednesday night.

Republican Sen. Connie Mack, travelling in Florida with Dole, refused to confirm or deny that Reed and Perot had met. But he added: "Anytime you can pick up a few points here or there it is worth the effort."

Perot's candidacy has attracted little enthusiasm -- polls show his support varying between 6 percent and 8 percent -- but he continues to siphon off votes from the major candidates, particularly Dole.

With less than two weeks before the Nov. 5 election, the Republican candidate took a triple punch from polls in the key states of California, Michigan and Ohio on Wednesday as he renewed an attack on Clinton's ethics.

In a campaign message broadcast on CNN, Dole returned to a theme he sounded last week, alleging that the Clinton administration was riddled with people who had committed criminal acts and impropriaties.
"How can a president lead Americans when he is the source of our cynicism? ... We have a duty to talk about this administration's public ethics because it is a matter of public trust," Dole said.
"Some people have asked the question: Do public ethics really matter? Today I am asking a different question: Could anything possibly matter more?" Dole said.

Three polls provided sombre news for Dole from key states. Reuters surveys said Clinton was leading Dole among likely voters by 14.5 percentage points in Michigan and by 11.6 points in Ohio. The Ohio news was especially ominous for Dole, since no Republican has become president without winning that state.
But the most devastating development was a Los Angeles Times poll's finding that Clinton led in California by 20 points, with only 13 days left until the Nov. 5 election.

Dole decided last week to concentrate much of his remaining resources on California -- the richest single political prize of all 50 states -- after another poll said he had cut Clinton's lead there to 10 points.

The Republican nominee sent several top campaign operatives to the state in a last-ditch effort to turn the election around and began spending heavily on television advertisements. California has some of the most expensive media markets in the country.
To pay for the blitz, Dole pulled his ads off the air in other key states, including New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
California, the most populous state, has 54 electoral votes -- one-fifth of the 270-vote Electoral College majority needed to win the presidency under the indirect U.S. system.
Ohio and Michigan account for a further 39 votes.
Both candidates were campaigning on Wednesday in Florida, usually a Republican bastion. But Clinton is narrowly leading there this year, thanks to his support among women and retirees.

Clinton, staying presidential, started the day with a round of golf before addressing a rally in Daytona Beach where he highlighted a government report showing that child support payments had risen 50 percent over the last four years.

"We're going to keep going until we raise child support more and more and more. We're going to move hundreds of thousands of people off welfare by making sure that the parents do what they ought to do -- take responsibility for their children and their future," he told a cheering crowd.

Dole, trying to keep his spirits up, has been telling supporters to ignore the polls. He started his day at a sparsely attended rally in Macon, Georgia, then flew to Panama City in the normally Republican Florida Panhandle.
"This is a state we must win. This is a state we should win," Dole said. "I'm a conservative. He's a liberal. Don't let him fool you."
